cards.front: In the canonical GPCR pathway, what three things together decide a cell's first response to a hormone?
cards.back: The GPCR subtype, the G protein it couples to, and the downstream proteins in that cell.
cards.why: The same hormone can therefore give opposite answers in different tissues.
cards.quote: GPCR subtype, G protein, and downstream proteins decide the first response.

cards.front: A G-protein-coupled receptor is one protein chain that crosses the plasma membrane {{c1::seven}} times.
cards.back: Each crossing is an alpha helix.
cards.quote: A G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) is one protein chain that crosses the plasma membrane seven times.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: In a GPCR, which end of the chain lies outside the cell and which inside?
cards.back: The amino end lies outside the cell; the carboxyl end lies inside.
cards.quote: The amino end lies outside the cell and the carboxyl end inside
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: Roughly {{c1::a third}} of approved drugs act on a GPCR.
cards.quote: Roughly a third of approved drugs act on a GPCR.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: In the beta-2-adrenergic receptor, what change inside the cell follows binding of a high-affinity agonist and Gs, and what does it open?
cards.back: The cytoplasmic end of helix 6 moves outward by about 14 angstroms, opening the cavity where the tail of G alpha docks.
cards.quote: the cytoplasmic end of helix 6 moves outward by about 14 angstroms, opening the cavity where the tail of G alpha docks
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: What are the three subunits of a heterotrimeric G protein, and which two act as one unit?
cards.back: G alpha, G beta and G gamma. G beta and G gamma bind so tightly that they act as one beta-gamma unit.
cards.quote: G beta and G gamma bind so tightly that they act as one beta-gamma unit.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: What holds a heterotrimeric G protein at the plasma membrane's inner face?
cards.back: Lipid tails on G alpha and G gamma.
cards.quote: Lipid tails on G alpha and G gamma hold the trio at the membrane's inner face
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: The active receptor acts as a guanine-nucleotide {{c1::exchange factor (GEF)}}: it promotes GDP release from G alpha.
cards.quote: The active receptor acts as a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): it promotes GDP release from G alpha
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: After a receptor promotes GDP release from G alpha, why does GTP rather than GDP fill the empty site?
cards.back: GTP is more plentiful than GDP in the cytosol, so it fills the empty site.
cards.quote: GTP, more plentiful than GDP in the cytosol, fills the empty site.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: In the exchange reaction on a G protein, why does the active receptor appear on both sides of the equation?
cards.back: It is a catalyst: it is not consumed, which is the source of gain.
cards.quote: The receptor appears on both sides because it is a catalyst
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: What event ends one activation cycle of a heterotrimeric G protein?
cards.back: G alpha hydrolyses GTP, and the GDP-bound trimer reforms.
cards.quote: One activation cycle ends when G alpha hydrolyses GTP and the GDP-bound trimer reforms.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: A mutant Gs alpha binds GDP but cannot release it. The receptor still binds agonist, and adenylyl cyclase works when forskolin stimulates it directly. What happens to agonist-driven cAMP, and why?
cards.back: It fails to rise. The receptor activates, but G alpha cannot release GDP to load GTP, so the G protein stays inactive.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that receptor-catalysed GDP release is the step that activates G alpha.
cards.quote: It fails. The receptor activates, but G alpha cannot release GDP to load GTP, so the G protein stays inactive.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: The human genome has {{c1::16}} G-alpha genes in four sequence families.
cards.quote: The human genome has 16 G-alpha genes in four sequence families.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: Name the four G-alpha families and the main direct target of each.
cards.back: Gs: adenylyl cyclase (activated). Gi/o: adenylyl cyclase (inhibited). Gq/11: phospholipase C-beta. G12/13: exchange factors for Rho.
cards.quote: The human genome has 16 G-alpha genes in four sequence families.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: What are the first consequences of Gq/11 activating phospholipase C-beta?
cards.back: PIP2 becomes IP3 and DAG, and calcium rises.
cards.quote: The human genome has 16 G-alpha genes in four sequence families.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: What is the first consequence of G12/13 activating its targets?
cards.back: Exchange factors for Rho act, actin rearranges, and cells change shape and move.
cards.quote: The human genome has 16 G-alpha genes in four sequence families.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: In heart pacemaker cells, how does Gi activation slow firing by way of its beta-gamma pair?
cards.back: Beta-gamma released from Gi opens the GIRK potassium channel. Potassium flows out and moves the membrane potential away from the firing threshold.
cards.quote: Beta-gamma is a signal too: in heart pacemaker cells, beta-gamma released from Gi opens the GIRK potassium channel
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: Besides beta-gamma opening GIRK, how does G-alpha-i slow pacemaker cells?
cards.back: It lowers cAMP, which reduces current through pacemaker channels that cAMP opens directly.
cards.quote: G-alpha-i also lowers cAMP, reducing current through pacemaker channels that cAMP opens directly.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: What does pertussis toxin do to G alpha-i and G alpha-o, and what is the result for the G protein?
cards.back: It adds ADP-ribose to a cysteine near the tail, so the tail cannot engage the receptor and the protein stays GDP-bound.
cards.quote: adds ADP-ribose to a cysteine near the tail of G alpha-i and G alpha-o, so the tail cannot engage the receptor and the protein stays GDP-bound
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: In a cultured cell line, an agonist lowers cAMP. Pertussis toxin leaves basal cAMP unchanged and the agonist still binds, but cAMP no longer falls. Which G-alpha family carried the response?
cards.back: Gi/o. The toxin stops the receptor from activating Gi/o, so the fall in cAMP is lost while basal cAMP is not.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a response abolished by pertussis toxin most likely runs through Gi/o.
cards.quote: If pertussis toxin abolishes a response, that response most likely runs through Gi/o.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: A response is not blocked by pertussis toxin. Why does that not exclude Gi/o-family signaling?
cards.back: Gz, a Gi/o-family member, lacks the toxin site, so toxin resistance does not exclude that family. The test is strong in one direction only.
cards.quote: Gz, a Gi/o-family member, lacks the toxin site, so toxin resistance does not exclude that family.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: How does cholera toxin differ from pertussis toxin in its effect on a G protein?
cards.back: Cholera toxin jams Gs on, whereas pertussis toxin keeps Gi/o in its GDP-bound, receptor-deaf state.
cards.quote: Cholera toxin, from the lesson on GTPase switches, instead jams Gs on.
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: Intestinal cells are treated with cholera toxin, which prevents Gs alpha from hydrolysing GTP. Why does cAMP stay high after the hormone is removed?
cards.back: Gs alpha stays GTP-bound and keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase, so the activation cycle never ends.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that an activation cycle ends only when G alpha hydrolyses GTP.
cards.quote: One activation cycle ends when G alpha hydrolyses GTP and the GDP-bound trimer reforms.
cards.section: From an outside pocket to an inside switch

cards.front: Acetylcholine slows the heartbeat but contracts airway smooth muscle. What differs between the two tissues?
cards.back: The receptor subtype and G protein: M2 with Gi in pacemaker cells, M3 with Gq in airway muscle.
cards.quote: through M2 and Gi it slows pacemaker cells, and through M3 and Gq it contracts airway muscle
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: At skeletal muscle, acetylcholine also acts, but the 'subtype decides' rule does not apply there. Why not?
cards.back: There acetylcholine meets an ion channel, not a GPCR.
cards.quote: at skeletal muscle it meets an ion channel from the receptor field guide, not a GPCR
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: Which G-alpha family do the alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta adrenergic subtypes couple to, mainly?
cards.back: Alpha-1 to Gq, alpha-2 to Gi, beta to Gs.
cards.quote: Three alpha-1 subtypes couple mainly to Gq, three alpha-2 subtypes to Gi, and three beta subtypes to Gs.
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: Adrenaline makes the heart beat harder, relaxes airway muscle and narrows skin vessels. Assign an adrenergic subtype and G-alpha family to each tissue.
cards.back: Heart: beta-1 on Gs. Airway muscle: beta-2 on Gs. Skin vessels: alpha-1 on Gq, because raised cytosolic calcium contracts smooth muscle.
cards.why: Rests on the receptor-to-family couplings of the three adrenergic classes.
cards.quote: Skin vessels: alpha-1 on Gq, because raised cytosolic calcium contracts smooth muscle.
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: Heart and airway cells both use beta receptors on Gs and raise cAMP, yet respond oppositely. Why?
cards.back: Different downstream proteins wait for cAMP in each cell type, so they interpret the same messenger differently.
cards.quote: Heart and airway cells interpret the same messenger differently because different downstream proteins wait for cAMP
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: A drug blocks only beta-1 receptors during adrenaline signaling. Predict the effects on heart and airway, and say what changes if the drug also blocks beta-2.
cards.back: Heartbeat rate and force fall, and airway and vessel receptors are untouched. Also blocking beta-2 removes adrenaline's airway relaxation, a risk for a person with asthma.
cards.why: Rests on beta-1 acting in heart and beta-2 in airway muscle.
cards.quote: A blocker that also hits beta-2 removes adrenaline's airway relaxation, a risk for a person with asthma.
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: The thrombin receptor on platelets activates both Gq and G12/13. A drug blocks only the Gq branch. Which output could remain?
cards.back: The G12/13 output: Rho exchange factors can still reshape the cell, even if the Gq-dependent calcium rise is lost.
cards.quote: The G12/13 branch could still activate Rho exchange factors and reshape the cell
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: Define basal activity, and say how an agonist, a neutral antagonist and an inverse agonist each move it.
cards.back: Basal activity is a receptor population's signaling with no ligand. An agonist raises it, a neutral antagonist leaves it while blocking other ligands, and an inverse agonist lowers it.
cards.quote: an agonist raises it, a neutral antagonist leaves it while blocking other ligands, an inverse agonist lowers it.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: Why did many drugs long called antagonists turn out to be inverse agonists?
cards.back: For many receptors only a small fraction is active at once, so basal activity is too low to measure. Tested where it is visible, the drugs lowered it.
cards.quote: Many drugs long called antagonists proved to be inverse agonists once tested where it was visible.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: Cells lacking a Gs-coupled receptor make cAMP at 10 pmol per minute. Cells expressing it make 30 pmol per minute with no ligand. Drug R lowers the expressing cells to 12 pmol per minute and does nothing in cells lacking the receptor. Classify R and state what fraction of the receptor's own basal signaling it removes.
cards.back: Inverse agonist, removing 90%. Receptor-driven basal output is 30 - 10 = 20. R leaves 12 - 10 = 2 of those 20, so it removes 18 of 20.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that an inverse agonist lowers basal activity.
cards.quote: an agonist raises it, a neutral antagonist leaves it while blocking other ligands, an inverse agonist lowers it.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: Agonist A gives 100 units of cAMP at saturation; ligand B gives 35 units alone and lowers A's response from 100 to 50 when added at high concentration. Both compete for one site. How is B best classified, and is it a neutral antagonist or an inverse agonist?
cards.back: B is a partial agonist: it activates with lower efficacy than A and so reduces A's response. It raises output alone, so it is neither a neutral antagonist nor an inverse agonist.
cards.why: Rests on the efficacy rule: an agonist raises activity, an inverse agonist lowers it.
cards.quote: efficacy, how far a bound ligand moves the response, can also push it below where it started.
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers

cards.front: Drug X shifts an agonist's EC50 from 2 nM to 20 nM with 10 nM X present, but high agonist doses still give the full 100 units, and X alone does not change basal cAMP. What is X?
cards.back: A reversible competitive antagonist: the curve shifts right (10-fold in EC50) but the maximum is reached by raising agonist. It counts as neutral only if basal activity is measurable and unchanged.
cards.why: Basal activity can be too low to measure, so no change in basal cAMP alone cannot prove neutrality.
cards.quote: an agonist raises it, a neutral antagonist leaves it while blocking other ligands, an inverse agonist lowers it.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: A receptor couples to Gi/o in one cell line and is later found to signal through Gq in another. Why is a coupling measured in one cell line only a hypothesis about the next?
cards.back: One receptor can couple to several G-alpha families, and the dominant partner can differ between cell types.
cards.quote: one receptor can couple to several G-alpha families, and the dominant partner can differ between cell types
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: How does a GPCR that stays active for a long time get shut down?
cards.back: Kinases phosphorylate the receptor, then arrestin binds its tail, blocks further G-protein coupling and helps pull the receptor into the cell.
cards.quote: Kinases phosphorylate a receptor that has stayed active, then arrestin binds its tail, blocks further G-protein coupling and helps pull the receptor into the cell.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: Two cell lines have equal Gs-coupled receptor, but one lacks both beta-arrestins. After 15 minutes of saturating agonist, which line should show more cAMP, and why?
cards.back: The line lacking beta-arrestins. Its initial response can be normal, but it loses a major brake on repeated receptor-G-protein coupling, so desensitization is reduced.
cards.quote: Its initial response can be normal, but it loses a major brake on repeated receptor–G-protein coupling, so desensitization is reduced.
cards.section: Ligand efficacy, and why "GPCRs can be unfaithful to trimeric G proteins"

cards.front: How did two laboratories find seven stretches long enough to span a membrane in bovine rhodopsin?
cards.back: They cut rhodopsin at methionine and sequenced the pieces one amino acid at a time. The 1983 sequence had seven water-avoiding stretches long enough to span a membrane.
cards.quote: By 1983 both had published the complete cow-rhodopsin sequence, including seven water-avoiding stretches long enough to span a membrane.
cards.section: How the seven-pass plan was found

cards.front: The cloned beta-adrenergic receptor resembled rhodopsin, including seven spans. What did this show about the seven-pass plan?
cards.back: It marks receptors that signal through G proteins, not only light-sensitive molecules, since the adrenaline receptor does not use light.
cards.quote: The adrenaline receptor showed instead that it marked receptors that signal through G proteins.
cards.section: How the seven-pass plan was found

cards.front: Roughly how many GPCR genes does the human genome hold, and what makes up about half of them?
cards.back: Roughly 800 genes; about half are odorant receptors.
cards.quote: The human genome holds roughly 800 GPCR genes; Lefkowitz's Nobel lecture says almost a thousand.
cards.section: How many GPCR genes

cards.front: An orphan seven-pass receptor gene is expressed in cells lacking it. In forskolin-stimulated cells, a candidate ligand lowers cAMP from 100 to 40 units only in cells with the receptor, and pertussis toxin restores 100 units. What does this show, and by how much does the ligand lower cAMP?
cards.back: The receptor couples to Gi/o and the ligand is its agonist. The fall is 60 of 100 units, or 60%, only with the receptor, and pertussis toxin removes it.
cards.why: Rests on the pertussis test: loss of a cAMP fall after toxin places the response in Gi/o. Howlett's cannabinoid test worked this way.
cards.quote: Allyn Howlett's laboratory had shown that cannabinoids lower cAMP dose-dependently in nerve-cell preparations, that only one mirror-image form works, and that pertussis toxin blocks the effect.
cards.section: How the pertussis test named CB1

cards.front: A membrane patch from a pacemaker cell is exposed to purified Gi alpha with a non-hydrolysable GTP analogue (channel stays closed), then to purified beta-gamma (channel opens). Intact cells given pertussis toxin no longer open the channel to acetylcholine. What model fits?
cards.back: The receptor activates Gi, and the freed beta-gamma, not G alpha, then opens the potassium channel.
cards.why: Rests on the rules that pertussis toxin blocks receptor-to-Gi coupling and that beta-gamma released from Gi opens GIRK.
cards.quote: Beta-gamma is a signal too: in heart pacemaker cells, beta-gamma released from Gi opens the GIRK potassium channel
cards.section: "All the pathways": four G-alpha families, then many targets

cards.front: A hormone raises cytosolic calcium and PKC translocation in smooth muscle through a GPCR. A phospholipase C-beta inhibitor abolishes both, but a membrane-permeable DAG analogue still activates PKC. Which G-alpha family carries the hormone's signal, and where is the block?
cards.back: Gq/11: it activates phospholipase C-beta, which turns PIP2 into IP3 (calcium rise) and DAG (PKC). The block is at phospholipase C-beta, upstream of DAG.
cards.why: Rests on the Gq/11 row of the family table.
cards.quote: Skin vessels: alpha-1 on Gq, because raised cytosolic calcium contracts smooth muscle.
cards.section: One ligand, different cellular answers
